questions.q: What are the four AWS IAM object types that work together as one unified system?
options: Users, groups, roles, and policies
Subscriptions, resource groups, tenants, and directories
Accounts, organizational units, service control policies, and guardrails
Buckets, objects, keys, and regions
questions.explain: Users and groups are persistent identities, roles are assumed temporarily, and policies are the JSON documents defining what's allowed or denied — together these four object types make up AWS IAM's single, unified identity and authorization system.

questions.q: In an IAM policy statement, what does the "Action" field specify?
options: Exactly which API calls the statement covers (e.g., s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket)
Whether the statement should be enforced immediately or after a delay
The AWS region the policy applies to
The human-readable name of the policy
questions.explain: Action lists the specific API operations the statement covers. In the lesson's example policy, Action is scoped narrowly to s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, so the identity cannot write, delete, or modify anything.

questions.q: What is the difference between an identity-based policy and a resource-based policy?
options: An identity-based policy is attached to a user, group, or role; a resource-based policy is attached directly to the resource itself, like an S3 bucket policy
Identity-based policies only apply to AWS services, never to human users
Resource-based policies can only deny access, never allow it
There is no real difference -- the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: Identity-based policies define what a given user, group, or role can do, while resource-based policies (like an S3 bucket policy) are attached to the resource and define who is allowed to access that specific resource, regardless of which identity is asking.

questions.q: What is a role's "trust policy" for?
options: It defines who is allowed to assume the role -- a separate document from the role's permissions policy
It defines what actions the role can perform once assumed
It is only used for resource-based policies, never for roles
It automatically expires the role's permissions every 24 hours
questions.explain: A role always has two documents: the trust policy, which defines who (what principal) may assume the role, and the permissions policy, which defines what the role is allowed to do once assumed. The lesson's trust policy example restricts assumption to a specific account with a matching external ID.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say IAM roles are more governance-friendly than long-lived IAM user access keys?
options: A role's temporary credentials expire automatically (often within an hour), bounding the damage window if they leak, while a leaked long-lived key remains a standing risk until someone notices and revokes it
Roles are always free, while long-lived access keys incur additional AWS charges
Long-lived access keys cannot be used with any AWS service except S3
Roles eliminate the need for any policy document at all
questions.explain: AWS's own current best-practice guidance favors roles assumed via STS over long-lived user access keys specifically because role credentials expire on their own, limiting exposure if they're ever compromised -- a leaked long-lived key keeps working until someone actively revokes it.
